summary: The light bench traces rays through real surfaces: at each one a ray bends by Snell's law or reflects, with the glass's refractive index from its published Sellmeier formula. The lens equation's image distance, the prism's deviation and a light guide's acceptance angle are checked against the traced rays. The bench is flat, white light is nine wavelengths, and the weak reflections at glass surfaces are left out.

claims.claim: Rays bend by Snell's law, n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, and reflect totally past the critical angle.
claims.how: Refraction uses the vector form of Snell's law; when it has no solution the ray reflects (total internal reflection).

sources.title: Snell's law
sources.says: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂; in vector form v_refract = rℓ + (rc − √(1 − r²(1 − c²)))n with r = n₁/n₂ and c = −n·ℓ; beyond θ_crit = arcsin(n₂/n₁) light is totally reflected.

claims.note: Checked at six angles and three wavelengths, to 9 decimal places; the critical angle in its own test.

claims.claim: The glass is Schott N-BK7 and N-SF11, with their published Sellmeier coefficients.
claims.how: n² − 1 = Σ Bᵢλ² / (λ² − Cᵢ), with the data sheets' six coefficients for each glass.
claims.note: nd, nF and nC of N-BK7 to 4 decimal places, and its Abbe number 64.17.

claims.claim: A lens's focal length follows the lensmaker's equation, and its image the lens equation 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i.
claims.how: The bench prints f from the thick-lens lensmaker's equation and d_i from the lens equation (measured from the principal planes), beside where the traced rays from the object's foot, close to the axis, really cross.

sources.title: Lens
sources.says: 1/f = (n − 1)[1/R₁ − 1/R₂ + (n − 1)d/(nR₁R₂)]; and the Gaussian lens formula 1/f = 1/S₁ + 1/S₂ (virtual images have negative S₂).

claims.note: For the four lenses at three object distances the traced image is within 0.3% of the formula. Rays far from the axis cross a little off it (spherical aberration and the aberrations of off-axis points), as with real lenses.

claims.claim: A prism deviates light by δ = i + e − A, more for blue than for red, so white light fans out.
claims.how: The traced ray's change of direction is compared with the formula from Snell's law at each face, for two glasses, three angles and five wavelengths.

sources.title: Minimum deviation
sources.says: δ = i + e − A; at minimum deviation n = sin((A + D_m)/2) / sin(A/2), when the ray inside runs parallel to the base.

claims.note: Agreement to 1e-9 radian; N-BK7's minimum deviation at 587.6 nm for a 60° prism is 38.65°.

claims.claim: A concave mirror focuses a parallel beam at f = R / 2; a flat mirror reflects at the angle it was hit.
claims.how: Rays near the axis are traced off a circular mirror and their crossing with the axis is measured.

sources.title: Focal length
sources.says: For a spherically curved mirror, the magnitude of the focal length is equal to the radius of curvature of the mirror divided by two.

claims.claim: The light guide keeps light inside by total internal reflection, accepting rays up to the angle its numerical aperture gives.
claims.how: A core of N-SF11 in a cladding of N-BK7: the critical angle is arcsin(n₂/n₁) and the acceptance half angle arcsin(√(n₁² − n₂²)) in air; rays are traced into a straight guide at angles either side of it.

sources.title: Numerical aperture
sources.says: For a step-index fiber NA = √(n_core² − n_clad²), and n sin θ_max = NA gives the acceptance angle.

claims.note: A tight bend lets light out where it meets the wall under the critical angle; the bend radius is an option.

simplified: The bench is flat: rays travel in one plane, and lenses and mirrors are their cross sections.
White light is drawn as nine wavelengths from 410 to 665 nm, and the colors on screen are approximations of the spectral colors.
The weak reflections at each glass surface (about 4% for N-BK7 face on) are left out; only refraction, mirror reflection and total internal reflection are drawn.
The light guide is a thick glass rod with a high-index core (N-SF11 in N-BK7), much wider than a telecom fiber, so its rays can be seen; it works by the same total internal reflection.
